Chapter 2 Using HumanIslets.com The platforms left-hand navigation groups features into four blocks  Omics, Donor & Phenotype, Search & Discovery, and Data Download. This chapter is organized in the same order, with one section per page in the sidebar. 2.1 Omics The Omics block holds the analyses that operate primarily on feature-level molecular data: differential-expression-style omics analysis and multi-omics integration. 2.1.1 Omics View HumanIslets.com presently includes information from 650 human research islet isolations that includes donor and technical metadata, islet and islet cell function, and omics. The Omics Type menu offers Bulk gene expression (RNA-seq), Bulk gene expression (Nanostring), Bulk protein expression, Pseudobulk gene expression, Single-cell gene expression (patch-seq), Environmental contaminants, Metabolite intensity, DNA Methylation and Metabolic flux simulation. Omics-metadata relationships can be analysed by: Selecting the Omics Type of interest For Bulk protein expression, a second menu selects Batch 1, Batch 2 or Combined. For Combined, choose Batch corrected (ComBat) or Batch as covariate (batch is added to the model automatically). Selecting the Primary Metadata to be analysed, and Comparison of Interest if applicable Choosing covariates to control for Many covariates are available for correction and selection may depend on comparisons being made or the objective of the user. Note however we have reported important impacts of correcting for culture time, particularly when examining RNAseq data, and Non-endocrine cell proportion (computed) when comparing groups with dramatically different preparation purities. Selecting donors to include Choosing Subset will open a window that allows for filtering by donor characteristics and data availability, or upload of a list of donor IDs or RRIDs of interest Selecting a p-value cutoff, and the use of adjusted p-values Click submit The number of donors included in the analysis will be displayed. If too few donors are available for the chosen analysis (<10), an error message will be shown. Results of the analysis will be shown under Feature Association Results. Results can be downloaded with Download Results, and Save Analysis saves the analysis (its R code and input data) so it can be rerun locally. Results are shown as a graphical representation (volcano plot) or table, accessible by clicking on the appropriate tab. Clicking on features (points in the volcano plot, or table entries) will raise a graph showing categorical or scatterplot representations of the data/feature of interest. Clicking on individual donors within those plots will take you to the Donor View page for that donor, allowing for inspection of potential outlier donors. At the right are links to the NCBI gene page and T2D Knowledge Portal (T2DKP) entries for each feature (external sites), to a single-cell RNAseq reference dataset (SC) to inspect cell-type specific expression of the feature, and to IsletAgent (KG link; section 2.3.1) for the evidence about the feature. The Associated proportions column flags genes whose RNA-seq level is linked to the non-endocrine cell proportion: Non-endocrine (higher when there are more non-endocrine cells), Endocrine (lower), or None. This helps spot features that may reflect islet purity rather than the comparison of interest. Wilcoxon check. For a two-group comparison with no covariates, the results table also shows a Wilcoxon rank-sum test next to limma, as a check that does not assume normally distributed data. Three columns are added at the end: Wilcoxon AUC (the chance that a donor in one group has a higher value than a donor in the other; above 0.5 means higher in the group where log2FC is positive, and 0.5 means no difference), Wilcoxon p_value and Wilcoxon adjusted p_value. The check runs only when both groups have enough donors, and not for DNA methylation. Because the Wilcoxon test cannot adjust for covariates, it is not shown when covariates are selected, including the batch covariate that is added automatically for some datasets. DNA methylation is analysed with the same association framework, but at the level of individual CpG sites rather than genes: differential analysis is run on M-values (log2 methylation ratios), while the per-feature boxplots show -values (the 01 methylation proportion). Each result row shows the CpGs genomic location, its annotated gene, and its CpG-island relation. Methylation is profiled at roughly 729,000 CpG sites, so the analysis takes a little longer than other omics, and a methylation-only Regions (DMR) tab additionally groups neighbouring CpGs into differentially methylated regions. The third tab under the Feature Association Results pulls up a Pathway Analysis tool. The enrichment method offered depends on the omics type, because gene-based, metabolite-based, and reaction-based feature lists each require matched annotation libraries: Gene-based omics (RNA-seq, Nanostring, proteomics, pseudobulk, patch-seq): Overrepresentation Analysis (ORA) and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) against KEGG, Reactome, GO, and the GEM gene libraries. DNA methylation: gene-set ORA and GSEA, run through a methylation-aware engine: each CpG is mapped to its annotated gene(s) and the enrichment is corrected for the number of CpG probes per gene (genes covered by more probes would otherwise be biased toward looking enriched). ORA uses missMethyls gsameth and GSEA uses methylGSA, against the same gene-based libraries (KEGG, Reactome, GO, and the GEM gene sets); reaction-level GEM sets do not apply. Metabolomics: MSEA (Metabolite Set Enrichment Analysis), the metabolomics analogue of GSEA, implemented via xialabs MetaboAnalyst and ranking metabolites against curated metabolite sets (KEGG human metabolite-centred pathways and the GEM metabolite groupings). Metabolic flux: RSEA (Reaction Set Enrichment Analysis), ranking reactions against Human-GEM subsystem groupings (glycolysis, TCA cycle, fatty-acid metabolism, etc.). This is the analogue of GSEA at the reaction level. To perform pathway / metabolite / reaction analysis: Select ORA or GSEA / MSEA / RSEA as appropriate for the omics type ORA is performed on significant hits based on the p-value threshold set above GSEA / MSEA / RSEA can be performed using log2FC/coefficient or T-statistic for ranking, and can be performed even in cases when no individual features are marked as significant Select whether to collapse redundant pathways / sets Choose a false discovery rate (FDR) cutoff Choose among the available libraries for the matched omics type Click submit The Pathway Results will be displayed in both graphical and table format, selected by clicking on the appropriate tab. As above, results can be downloaded with Download Results, and Save Analysis saves the analysis so it can be rerun locally. In the interactive graphical view, significant pathways (based on FDR cutoff) are shown as ridgeplots. Clicking on these will raise heatmaps showing the contribution of individual genes/proteins. 2.1.2 Multi-omics View The Multi-omics View lets users explore integrated analyses across two or three omics layers selected from a single dropdown (WGCNA and MOFA results are precomputed for combinations where at least 20 donors have every selected omics type). Three complementary methods are available, each answering a slightly different question and unlocked by selecting it from the Method dropdown: WGCNA (Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis) is unsupervised. It groups features that move together across donors into modules, then summarises each module by a single representative value (its eigengene) so that module-level signal can be compared across omics and against the platforms phenotype variables. Use WGCNA when the question is which features behave like a co-regulated programme, and does any module track a phenotype? MOFA (Multi-Omics Factor Analysis) is also unsupervised, but rather than discrete modules it learns continuous latent factors  directions of variation that several omics share. The same factor often explains a substantial chunk of variance in two or more views, which makes MOFA a good fit when the goal is to find the shared axes of variation across omics types. Donors with only partial omics coverage are still usable thanks to MOFAs NA-tolerant fit. DIABLO (Data Integration Analysis for Biomarker discovery using Latent cOmponents) is supervised: it requires a primary metadata variable as the target and finds the smallest set of correlated features across omics that best discriminates two groups (or predicts a continuous outcome). Use DIABLO when the question is phrased as which combined feature signature best separates these donor groups? A help (?) tooltip next to the dropdown summarises these three methods inline. Full methodology and parameter choices are in chapter 5; here we walk through how to use each method on the page. To run a multi-omics analysis: Pick the Method (WGCNA, MOFA, or DIABLO) from the dropdown Choose Omics Type I and Omics Type II (and optionally Omics Type III). For WGCNA and MOFA, results exist only for combinations with at least 20 shared donors; other combinations show a Not Found message. DIABLO needs at least 10 shared donors with a value for the primary metadata. For patch-seq, an extra cell type selector appears ( /  /  / PP) For metabolite and flux, an extra glucose condition selector appears (low / high / ratio) For DIABLO only, pick a Primary Metadata variable and (for binary outcomes) the two contrast levels, and optionally covariates under Adjust for. WGCNA and MOFA are unsupervised and skip this step. Choose Donors: All, or Subset to use the donor filter Click Submit The result tabs (described below per method) then become available. WGCNA and MOFA results load almost instantly because they are precomputed; DIABLO runs when you click Submit and can take longer. WGCNA results layout. A summary bar shows the number of donors, features and modules, and the scale-free fit and power. Five tabs: Overview  a heatmap with modules on the rows and core phenotypes on the columns. Each cell shows the modulephenotype association: Pearson r (signed, 1 to +1) for continuous and binary phenotypes, or ANOVA-derived effect size (unsigned, 0 to 1) for multi-level categoricals. Cells carry significance asterisks (* padj<0.05, ** <0.01, *** <0.001), and hovering any cell reveals the full r / p / padj / n. A Select Phenotypes button opens a dialog to choose which phenotypes appear on the columns (with a Reset to defaults shortcut), and the heatmap can be exported as PNG (image) or CSV (underlying matrix). This is the entry-point view for which module tracks which phenotype, at a glance. Trait Associations  drill-down view for a single phenotype chosen from the Group / Phenotype selectors; shows that phenotypes association across every module in the combination (not just the curated core phenotype set in the Overview). Features  per-module feature table with module membership ranking and omics-type tags. Network  interactive node/edge view of the top topological-overlap edges, with nodes coloured by omics type and modules. Pathway  ORA or GSEA (ranked by kME) for a selected module. MOFA results layout. Seven tabs: Overview  a heatmap with MOFA factors on the rows and core phenotypes on the columns, using the same conventions as the WGCNA Overview: Pearson r for continuous/binary, effect size for multi-level categoricals, the same asterisk-based significance markers, the same hover detail, the same Select Phenotypes / Reset / PNG / CSV controls. This is the place to start when asking which MOFA factor tracks which phenotype. Variance Decomposition  per-factor per-view variance heatmap. Trait Associations  drill-down view for a single phenotype across every MOFA factor (analogue of WGCNAs Trait Associations tab). Feature Loadings  top-weighted features per factor per omics. Circos Plot  the top-loading features of a factor in each omics, linked by their correlation. Factor Space  donors plotted in factor space, with metadata-colouring options. Pathway  pathway enrichment for a selected factor. DIABLO results layout. Four tabs: Overview  Sample View (donors on the multi-omics components) and Total Variance (variance explained per component and omics). Important Features  loading plots per omics and the table of selected features, by component. Circos Plot  the selected features across omics, linked by their correlation. Pathway Analysis  ORA / GSEA on the selected features against the standard pathway libraries. All tables are downloadable as CSV from the corresponding tab. 2.2 Donor & Phenotype The Donor & Phenotype block groups the views that browse the cohort at the donor level: per-donor profiles, phenotype-only exploration, and multi-omics-derived donor stratification. 2.2.1 Donor View The Donor View page allows examination of individual donor, islet isolation, and functional data from each of 650 donors currently in the HumanIslets.com database. Donors can be searched by ADI IsletCore Donor ID or Research Resource ID (RRID). Data categories can be selected from the left-hand menu, organized into four groups: Metadata (Donor Information, Isolation Information); Genetic Variables (Ancestry, Genetic Risk Score); Insulin Secretion (Static GSIS plus separate Dynamic Insulin Response views for Glucose, Leucine, and Palmitate); and Other (Prohormone Expression, Mitochondrial Function, Single-cell electrophysiology, Pancreas Lipid Extraction, and Omics Availability). These metadata are described in detail in chapters 3 and 4, below. Typically, data is shown for selected donor in the context of the entire dataset, allowing for easy inspection and determination of whether a donor falls within the normal range of the population. A few points that are worth noting here: Donor Information shows the RRID if available. Clicking on this will link out to the NCBI Biosample page for this donor Isolation Information also contains the current inventory of snap frozen and cryopreserved islet tubes for that donor (all donors also have paraffin embedded biopsies) Isolation Information also shows dithizone-stained islet images taken after isolation and before distribution, when available Isolation Information includes cell type composition calculated by deconvolution in donors with bulk proteomics data (see section 5.6, below) Ancestry renders the donors ancestry as a donut chart with primary ancestry on the outer ring and secondary (sub-) ancestry on the inner ring (1000 Genomes-aligned), accompanied by tables of the underlying probabilities Genetic Risk Score shows the T1D Genetic Risk Score and the T2D Polygenic Risk Score, each with the donors overall score and position in the cohort distribution, plus partitioned risk (T1D: HLA DR-DQ, HLA class I, HLA class II and non-HLA; T2D: Hard or Soft clustering) Dynamic Insulin Responses can be shown with or without normalisation to baseline Mitochondrial Function (oxygen consumption by Seahorse assay) can be shown with or without normalisation to DNA and baseline Prohormone Expression shows the donors C-peptide, proinsulin, and proinsulin:C-peptide ratio concentrations as values plus per-readout cohort histograms, with a selector to switch between the measured conditions Pancreas Lipid Extraction shows the donors total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), and free cholesterol (FC) (mg/g tissue) as values plus per-lipid cohort histograms 2.2.2 Phenotype View The Phenotype View lets users probe relationships among the phenotype variables in the database (donor characteristics, isolation outcomes, secretion, mitochondrial function, perifusion, electrophysiology) without selecting any omics type. The page has a left-hand menu with three options: Overview: a scrollable heatmap of every donor against every phenotype variable, with cells coloured by each donors z-score against the population, so at a glance users can see where a donor sits across the full phenotype panel and spot clusters of donors that look similar across many measurements at once. A Visual Filter radio group lets users restrict the view to a specific Donor subset (chosen via the standard donor filter dialog, by characteristics, data availability, or a donor-ID upload) or to a Phenotype subset (chosen via the phenotype filter dialog); clicking Update re-renders the heatmap with the chosen filter, and once a donor subset is applied a Download Donor List button appears so the same selection can be re-used on the Data Download page. Use this view to spot outliers, compare a few donors against the whole cohort, or quickly check which phenotype variables are populated for a candidate analysis cohort. Correlation: an interactive chord diagram (and matching sortable table) of pairwise correlations among phenotype variables, kept only when they pass a user-set correlation-magnitude cutoff and a p-value cutoff. Users can restrict the analysis to a subset of donors or phenotypes and choose whether to include within-group correlations (off by default so the chord emphasises cross-group co-variation), then click Submit. The results panel has two tabs: Chord Diagram  clicking any ribbon opens the scatter plot of the underlying donor-level values for that pair, so users can immediately see whether the correlation is driven by a linear trend, by an outlier cluster, or by something more complex; the dialog supports CSV / SVG / PNG / PDF export. Correlation Table  every kept pair listed in a sortable, searchable table (green / red colour-coded for positive vs. negative r); clicking a row opens the same scatter dialog, and a Download CSV button exports the full list. Use this view to find phenotype variables that strongly co-vary, for example which insulin-secretion measures track each other or whether HbA1c correlates with electrophysiology readouts. Phenotype PCA: Probabilistic PCA (PPCA) on the donor × phenotype matrix, which (unlike standard PCA) tolerates the missing-value pattern typical of phenotype data. Users pick which two principal components to plot, a Color by variable to colour the donor points (two-tier selector with variable group  variable name, mirroring the Omics page; continuous variables get a gradient, categorical variables a discrete palette), and optionally one categorical Shape by variable so two metadata dimensions can be encoded on the same scatter at once. Two additional controls fine-tune the fit  Label outliers (how many donors to label automatically by distance from the centroid) and Min samples (minimum non-missing measurements per phenotype to be included). After clicking Submit, the results panel has two tabs: PCA Plot  donors in PC space, coloured / shaped per the chosen variables. Clicking any donor point opens a Donor Profile dialog showing the top 10 phenotype features where that donor deviates most from the population mean (blue = above, orange = below). Feature Loadings  every phenotypes loading on the chosen PCs, ranked by importance (sum of |loadings| on the two PCs), with a Show top N selector and CSV export. Use this view to identify the major axes of phenotypic variation in the cohort, to spot outlier donors, and to see which phenotype variables drive that separation. 2.2.3 Cluster View The Cluster View groups donors into molecular clusters. The clusters come from bulk RNA-seq and proteomics, not from clinical labels. Donors without these omics data are assigned to a cluster from their phenotypes, and each assignment has a reliability level (high, medium or low). The full method is described in chapter 5 (Variational Autoencoder (VAE) for donor clustering). The page is called Cluster View in the sidebar, with the subtitle Donor cluster explorer. Donor map. The map shows every donor. Each cluster has its own arm, and a donor sits nearer the clusters it belongs to more strongly: omics donors from their omics data, and donors without omics from their predicted probabilities. Clicking a donor point opens that donors de-identified record. Color by / Shape by: colour the points by any phenotype or by cluster, and shape them by a categorical phenotype or by cluster. Measured (omics) / Predicted: click either legend item to show or hide those donors. Point size: sets the size of the points. Use the buttons to zoom in, zoom out or reset; scroll to zoom and drag to pan. Phenotype directions: a button shows which measured phenotypes vary across the map, as labels around it. Border donors: highlights measured donors that sit between two clusters. Cluster cards. A card on the right summarises each cluster: its name, a short description, the main phenotype and omics differences, and how many donors are measured or predicted. Selecting a card opens the cluster detail page (below). Comparing two groups. The Omics DE and Phenotype buttons open a panel that compares two groups of donors. Click a cluster to add it to Group A or Group B; Group B can also be all other clusters. For Omics DE, choose the omics type: RNA-seq, Proteomics, Nanostring, Pseudobulk (alpha), Pseudobulk (beta), Metabolomics (LG), Metabolomics (HG), Metabolomics (HG/LG) or Methylation. Advanced options let you adjust for covariates (regressed out with a linear model in limma), choose which donors to include (Omics only, + High conf., + High & Med or + All predicted), and limit donors with filters. Click Run to start, or Clear to start over. Cluster phenotype heatmap. Rows are phenotypes, grouped by category, and columns are clusters. Each cell shows Cohens d for the cluster against all other clusters (red = higher, blue = lower), with asterisks marking significance. Only phenotypes that reach nominal significance in at least one cluster are shown. The Donors filter sets which donors are used: Omics only, + High conf., + High & Med or + All predicted. Explore Further: cards linking to Cluster View, Omics Analysis, Multi-omics and IsletAgent. 2.3 Search & Discovery The Search & Discovery block groups feature-centric and entity-centric exploration: ask a question about a gene or phenotype, look up islet genetic associations, or jump from one feature to all its associations. 2.3.1 IsletAgent IsletAgent answers plain-language questions about a gene, a phenotype, or the relationship between them. Each answer is grounded in the HumanIslets cohort, in public and local genetics, and in public knowledge, all held in the platforms knowledge graph (chapter 7). The page is labelled BETA. Asking a question. You can ask about genes, proteins, metabolites and islet phenotypes, and the links between them. For example: whether a feature is related to a phenotype or disease, how features or pathways differ between donor groups such as diabetes status or molecular clusters, or how well an omics layer predicts a phenotype. Type a question in the box and click Ask, or click one of the example questions under Try, such as Is GCK linked to type 2 diabetes?, What predicts HbA1c (%)? or Which pathways are enriched in type 2 diabetes in RNA-seq? Click Watch an example to see a full answer step by step. While IsletAgent works, a progress bar shows each step: Understood, Chose, Found, Ran and Result. How it works. IsletAgent is a small language model, fine-tuned on grounded examples from the knowledge graph and run privately on local hardware. It reads the question, picks the entities and a retrieval route, and fetches the evidence from the knowledge graph through reviewed query templates. When a question needs a new calculation, it calls one of the platforms analyses, such as differential expression, phenotype association, pathway enrichment, colocalization or Mendelian randomization. Every retrieval and calculation can be checked and reproduced. Reading an answer. Each answer names its source: the data, the analysis and the number of donors behind it. Evidence verdict: the card at the top names the relationship (for example, GCK  type 2 diabetes) and gives a one-word verdict (for example, Convergent). It lists which sources agree (cohort, genetics, public knowledge) and shows the evidence grade (Limited, Moderate, Strong or Very Strong) with its evidence score. The grade scores the relationship, not the gene alone. A low grade means there is little evidence so far, not that the link is wrong. Overview tab: the evidence, shown as panels. Each panel can be moved, widened, collapsed or closed, and its ? button explains it. Which panels appear depends on the question: Evidence profile: how much each kind of evidence contributes, against its maximum: Association, Prediction, cis-QTL, GWAS, Mendelian randomization and Knowledge. Donor-level measurement: each donors level of the feature, one panel per platform, split by the phenotype (for example, Diabetes diagnosis or Corrected diabetes status), with covariate-adjusted significance. Prediction: the multivariate models (random forest, XGBoost, elastic net) that rank the feature as a predictor, showing where it ranks and how well each model predicts. What the cohort holds: how many donors have the feature on each platform, and its distribution. Traits linked to : the traits most strongly associated with the gene in public genetics, with their HuGE evidence tier. Knowledge-graph context: only the curated public relations that link the two entities (PrimeKG, Hetionet and pathway libraries). Literature: published mentions, with PMID and title. These are pointers only; they are never scored and never sent to the model. Methods & data tab: Results: every result behind the answer as a table, with View and CSV. Methods and input data: the statistical method behind each calculation, the data it used, and an R script + data download that reproduces it locally. Cohort · differential is a limma linear model per feature, phenotype and platform, adjusted for age, sex, BMI and culture time (none for the metabolite and contaminant layers), with BenjaminiHochberg adjusted p-values. Cohort · prediction uses random forest, XGBoost and elastic net, with cross-validated or held-out model quality. Public endpoint: the tab also shows the endpoint that returns the same answer (POST https://dev.humanislets.com/kg-api/agent/ask). Guide: the Guide tab and Take a quick tour of this answer walk through each part of the answer. Limits. IsletAgent answers only from the data and analyses HumanIslets supports. When the evidence is unclear, it gives a cautious answer. Use it to find and weigh evidence, not as proof of a mechanism. 2.3.2 GIFT Genomic View The GIFT Genomic View looks up islet genetic associations from GIFT (Genotype & Islet Function Trans-omics), the Gloyn labs islet genetics resource: genome-wide associations with islet function traits (GWAS-in-a-dish) and islet cis-QTLs (eQTL, exon-level eQTL, sQTL, pQTL and caQTL). Variant positions use GRCh38 (hg38). Chapter 6 describes the data in the view and how the plots and the quick colocalisation test are built. Searching. Type one of the following and click Search; the page picks the view that fits: a variant, by rsID or genomic position (for example chr1:727233 or chr1:727233:G:A); a gene, by HGNC symbol or Ensembl ID; a phenotype, by its label (for example Static-secretion stimulation index). Gene results have three tabs: QTL Results: a locus plot of the genes QTL hits in its cis window, one colour per QTL type, with the lead variant of each feature marked. Click a colour in the legend to show or hide that type, click a point to open that variant, and use the toolbar to zoom or pan. A table below lists each association (source, feature, position, rsID, alleles, effect size, standard error, P, minor allele frequency, distance and lead variant), with a source filter. Function GWAS: for each islet function trait, the strongest GWAS variant in the genes cis window and its distance from the QTL lead variant. Colocalisation: whether the genes QTL and an islet trait share a causal variant, with a short guide to reading the colocalisation probabilities. If the gene is not in the published colocalisation results, a Quick test can be run for reference. Variant results list the associations at that variant, with links to dbSNP, UCSC and the T2D Knowledge Portal, in four tabs: Forest Plot, PheWAS Plot, Results Table and Regional Plot. The main covariate model is shown first; Show all covariate models adds the others. Phenotype results show a genome-wide Manhattan plot for the trait and a table of its top 1,000 variants; the Model menu switches the covariate model. The first search can take a little while to load. 2.3.3 Feature View Instead of running an analysis in the Omics View focused on a particular omics type and metadata variable, users can search for a feature of interest and pull up ALL associations for that particular feature of interest, corrected for common covariates (see section 5.5, below). Searchable features include genes, proteins, metabolites, contaminants, CpG sites and metadata variables. This allows rapid interrogation of precomputed results across all datasets. Searching for a gene/protein feature generates a table of results sorted by p-value. Searching for a metadata variable (e.g. BMI) generates a table of feature (gene/protein) results across all omics datasets, sorted by p-value. Clicking on rows and external links brings up categorical or scatterplots of the association, external pages for the feature of interest, or single-cell RNAseq expression for that feature. Because a large number of associations can be displayed, filtering of the metadata or omics type is enabled by clicking on the column title. 2.4 Data Download The Data Download page is a standalone top-level entry in the sidebar; it does not belong to one of the analytical categories above. 2.4.1 Data Download Most data at HumanIslets.com can be downloaded. Bulk RNA-seq, proteomics and genetic data are available on request until publication, and patch-seq data are reached through a separate link on the page. Donors of interest can be filtered by Donor Characteristics (see section 3.1) and/or data availability. Advanced filters allow selection of donors of interest by any metadata available. Donors of interest can also be selected by uploading a list of donor IDs (for example, donor IDs obtained from a particular Omics View analysis). Data can be downloaded as Comma separated values (.csv), text (.txt), R object (.rds), or in Excel format (.xlsx) within a zip file. To perform data download: Under Select Donors choose filtering parameters, upload a list of donor IDs Distribution of chosen donors compared with the entire dataset can be assessed by clicking on the icons at right Once donors of interest are selected/filtered, click submit to choose those donors The total number of donors chosen will be displayed Under Download Data Select the datasets of interest Select the data format The distribution of datasets selected, compared with the entire database, can be shown by clicking Summary Click Download

Chapter 3 Overview of Primary Metadata 3.1 Donor Characteristics Current coverage: 650 donors. De-identified donor characteristics, including HLA-typing, collected at the time of organ procurement are provided in a de-identified manner to the ADI IsletCore team by the organ procurement organisations. Users should be aware that some information, such as diabetes diagnosis, may not be clinically validated at the time of organ retrieval. Whenever possible, HbA1c measurements are performed directly by the ADI IsletCore using blood samples sent with the organ, and donors indicated as type 1 diabetes (T1D) are validated as much as possible through genetic testing, autoantibody testing, and immunohistochemical analysis. While the Donor Metadata diabetes diagnosis reflects the status indicated by the organ procurement organization, the Donor Metadata corrected diabetes status indicates a classification based on the totality of information available to the ADI IsletCore (including pre-diabetes defined as HbA1c between 5.7 and 6.5%, and non-diagnosed donors with HbA1c>6.5% as type 2 diabetes (T2D)). Available donor characteristics metadata include: Age (years), Diabetes duration (years), Sex, Donation Type (NDD, DCD, MAID), BMI, HbA1c (%), HLA A2 (Yes/No), Diabetes diagnosis, Corrected diabetes status, and Multi-omics cluster (the donors molecular cluster from the Cluster View). 3.2 Organ Characteristics and Processing Current coverage: 643 donors. Organ characteristic and processing metadata is recorded during the islet isolation by the ADI IsletCore lead technician. Cold ischemia time is calculated from the cross clamp time during organ procurement until the start of the isolation in Edmonton. Please note that some measures, such as organ consistency are subjective. Available organ characteristics and processing metadata include: Cold Ischemic Time (h), Pancreas weight (g), Fatty infiltration (Yes/No), Organ consistency (Soft, Normal, Fibrotic, Inconsistent), Collagenase supplier (Roche, VitaCyte, Serva, Sigma), Collagenase type (Liberase, Clzyme, Gold, NB1, Sigma, Other, Recombinant), Digestion time (min). 3.3 Isolation Outcomes Current coverage: 636 donors. Islet purity, islet equivalents (IEQ), % trapped, and islet particle index (IPI) are determined by the ADI IsletCore lead technician. Full details can be found here or in our IsletCore welcome booklet. Details on determining Insulin and DNA samples as part of our quality control can be found here. Available isolation outcomes metadata include: Total islet equivalents (IEQ), Islet equivalents per pancreas weight (IEQ/g), Purity (%), Trapped (%), Islet particle index, Insulin content (ug), DNA content (ug), Insulin:DNA ratio, Insulin per IEQ (ng/IEQ). 3.4 Cell Type Proportions Current coverage: 234 donors (proteomics-based deconvolution). Cell proportions are estimated based on deconvolution of bulk islet proteomic data from hand-picked islets using canonical proteins as markers (see below). Estimated cell type proportions are shown as either the non-endocrine cell proportion (of all cells) or as the proportion of the endocrine compartment only. Available cell type proportions metadata include: Non-endocrine cell proportion (computed), beta-cell proportion (of endocrine; computed), alpha-cell proportion (of endocrine; computed), delta-cell proportion (of endocrine; computed), and gamma-cell proportion (of endocrine; computed). 3.5 Cell Culture Outcomes Current coverage: 587 donors. Following isolation, islets are cultured prior to shipment and sample collection for assay. On the day of shipping/collection, islets are recounted to determine islet equivalents (IEQ) and islet particle index (IPI) after culture. Culture time is determined by the end of the isolation until approximately 9 am on a shipping/collection day. The % recovery is calculated as pre-shipment IEQ / post-isolation IEQ × 100. Post-culture samples are collected for insulin and DNA as described. Available cell culture outcomes metadata include: Culture time (h), Total islet equivalents after culture (IEQ), Percent IEQ recovery after culture (%), Islet particle index after culture, Insulin content after culture, Insulin:DNA ratio after culture, Insulin per IEQ after culture (ng/IEQ). 3.6 Static Insulin Secretion Current coverage: 524 donors. On the day of sample collection (see section 3.5, above) islets are handpicked to 100% purity and cultured overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. In triplicates, 15 hand-picked islets from each donor are pre-incubated at low glucose for 2 x 1 hours consecutively, and then sequentially treated with low glucose for 1 hour followed by high glucose 1 hour. Collected supernatant for low glucose, high glucose or insulin content are measured by ELISA (ALPCO STELLUX Chemiluminescence). For each donor, there are multiple glucose combinations that are used. Experimental details can be found here. Glucose pairs are: 1mM  10mM glucose 1mM  16.7mM glucose 2.8mM  16.7mM glucose Outliers were handled in two ways. Level 1) A single donor-level measurement was computed as the median of the three replicate measures. Using the median instead of the mean reduced the impact of replicate-level outliers on the data. Level 2) The donor-level values were filtered to remove those that were more than 4 standard deviations away from the mean of all donors on a log10 scale. This removed values that were many orders of magnitude different from the population. In the Data Download tool, the data are provided at the replicate level (before outlier removal), while Omics View analysis is performed on data subjected to both Level 1 and Level 2 outlier removal. Available static insulin secretion metadata include: Culture time before experiment (days), Insulin content (pg/ml), Secretion at 1 mM glucose (pg/ml), Secretion at 2.8 mM glucose (pg/ml), Secretion at 10 mM glucose (pg/ml), Secretion at 16.7 mM glucose (pg/ml), Stimulation index (1->10 mM glucose), Stimulation index (1->16.7 mM glucose), Stimulation index (2.8->16.7 mM glucose). 3.7 Islet Oxygen Consumption (Seahorse assay) Current coverage: 142 donors. At the ADI IsletCore, after an overnight culture, islets are hand-picked, and 70 islets per well are assayed in triplicate for each donor. Islets are placed in the center of the well and islet capture screens are used to keep islets in place. Plate is incubated at 37oC for 1 hour without CO2, after which the plate is placed in the Xfe24 analyzer (Agilent). Basal measurements are at 2.8mM glucose, while stimulation is at 16.7mM glucose. 5uM oligomycin, 3uM FCCP and 5uM of rotenone and antimycin A are used as indicated. All solutions are made using DMEM supplemented with 1% FBS, sodium pyruvate and L-glutamine. After the run is complete, islets are collected and a DNA assay is done to normalize data. A detailed protocol is here. Available islet oxygen consumption (Seahorse assay) metadata include: Non-mitochondrial OC, Basal respiration, ATP respiration, Proton leak, Max glucose respiration, Glucose-stimulated respiration, Max respiration, Spare capacity, Glucose-stimulated OCI, Glucose-stimulated spare capacity, ATP respiration (glucose-stim.), Bioenergetic Health Index, and BHI (glucose-stim.). 3.8 Dynamic Insulin Responses to Macronutrients Current coverage: 166 donors (glucose), 164 donors (leucine), 163 donors (oleate/palmitate). After shipment to the University of British Columbia, islets are hand picked and cultured in RPMI for 24-72hrs before the experiment to allow recovery from shipping. 65 islets are loaded per chamber and pre-incubated for 1 hour. Islets are stimulated with 6 or 15mM glucose, 5mM Leucine or 0.75mM Oleic acid/0.75mM palmitic acid as indicated. Samples are stored at -20oC until analysis with RIA. Full details are described in Kolic et al. (2024) Cell Metabolism. Available dynamic insulin responses to macronutrients metadata include: 3 mM Glucose baseline secretion (AUC), 15 mM Glucose-stimulated peak, 15 mM Glucose-stimulated secretion (AUC), 6 mM Glucose-stimulated secretion (AUC), 30 mM KCl-stimulated secretion, after glucose (AUC), 5 mM Leucine-stimulated peak secretion , 5 mM Leucine-stimulated secretion (AUC), 5 mM Leucine + 6 mM Glucose-stimulated secretion (AUC), 30 mM KCl-stimulated secretion, after leucine (AUC), 1.5 mM Oleate/palmitate-stimulated peak secretion, 1.5 mM Oleate/palmitate-stimulated secretion (AUC), 1.5 mM Oleate/palmitate _ 6 mM glucose-stimulated peak secretion, 30 mM KCl-stimulated secretion, after oleate palmitate (AUC). 3.9 Single-cell Function (electrophysiology) Current coverage: 406 donors. On the day of collection (see section 3.5 above) islets are hand-picked, dispersed to single cells and plated on 35 mm cell culture dishes as described here. 24-72 hours after plating, electrophysiology is performed by whole-cell patch-clamp using procedures and solutions outlined in publications here and here. For earlier donors, only total exocytosis in response to a series of 10 membrane depolarizations from -70 to 0 mV is reported. For more recent donors (from R305 onward) an expanded panel of electrophysiological measures is reported that include measures of cell size, exocytosis, voltage-dependent Ca2+ channel activity, and voltage-dependent-Na+ channel activity. Cell types are identified either by immunostaining (insulin/glucagon) or by single-cell RNA sequencing after the experiment. In the Omics analysis, analyses can be performed on either alpha- or beta-cells, at 1, 5 or 10 mM glucose. Available single-cell function metadata include: Size (pF), Total exocytosis (fF/pF), Early (RRP) exocytosis (fF/pF), Late exocytosis (fF/pF), Calcium entry (pC/pF), Early calcium current amplitude (pA/pF), Late calcium current amplitude (pA/pF), Sodium current amplitude (pA/pF), Half inactivation sodium current (mV). 3.10 Prohormone Expression Current coverage: 126 donors. Proinsulin and C-peptide are measured to assess insulin biosynthesis and the efficiency of prohormone processing in the beta cell. Both analytes are quantified in three sample types per donor: the supernatant from a low-glucose (LG; 2.8 mM) incubation, the supernatant from a high-glucose (HG; 16.7 mM) incubation, and an islet lysate reflecting total cellular content. These measurements are contributed by the lab of Dr. Bruce Verchere (University of British Columbia) and appear in the Donor View as a dedicated tab; samples are derived from islets isolated by the Alberta Diabetes Institute (ADI) IsletCore. Proinsulin is measured with the TECO proinsulin ELISA (cat. TE1012) and C-peptide with the Mercodia C-peptide ELISA (cat. 10-1136-01), each run according to the manufacturers protocol. Because neither kit is supplied with a large volume of zero-standard, PBS is used as the sample diluent for both assays. Samples are diluted to fall within the standard curve: for proinsulin, 1:1 (LG), 1:10 (HG), and 1:10 for earlier lysate samples or 1:200 for more recent lysate samples; for C-peptide, 1:5 (LG), 1:50 (HG), and 1:250 (lysate). For the proinsulin assay, the kit blocking buffer is not ready-to-use and is diluted 1:5 in zero-standard before use. Concentrations are reported in pM as three replicate measurements plus a per-donor average, and both the C-peptide-to-proinsulin and proinsulin-to-C-peptide ratios are provided for each sample type as a readout of processing efficiency. Available prohormone expression metadata include (each measured in the low-glucose (2.8 mM) GSIS supernatant, the high-glucose (16.7 mM) GSIS supernatant, and the islet lysate): C-peptide concentration (pM; three replicates plus average), proinsulin concentration (pM; three replicates plus average), C-peptide-to-proinsulin ratio, and proinsulin-to-C-peptide ratio. 3.11 Ancestry Current coverage: 404 donors. Donor DNA is extracted from acinar tissue and genotyped on the Illumina Omni2.5Exome BeadChip (~2.5M variants, V1.5 / V1.6 from October 2024 onward) at the Stanford Functional Genomics Core. Array-level QC requires minor allele frequency > 1%, SNP missing-genotype rate < 1%, donor missing-genotype rate < 3%, and reported-vs-genetic sex matching. The genotypes are then imputed against the NIH TOPMed reference panel via the BioData Catalyst TOPMed Imputation Server (variants called to GRCh38, aligned to the + strand, imputation quality R² > 0.3), yielding more than 41 million high-quality variants per donor. These imputed genotypes feed both the ancestry inference described here and the genetic risk scores in the next section. Genetic ancestry is inferred from the imputed genotypes using the Gloyn-lab GeneticAncestry pipeline (DOI:10.5281/zenodo.18157870). The pipeline first reduces the genotype matrix to its principal components, then classifies each donor with an ensemble of supervised models (Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost, LightGBM, and a multi-layer perceptron) trained on the 1000 Genomes high-coverage, unrelated sequencing samples (where ancestry is known). Two levels of ancestry assignment are produced and shown in the donors donut chart: Primary ancestry (super-population, 5 categories) on the outer ring of the donut, aligned with the 1000 Genomes primary populations. Secondary ancestry (sub-population, 26 categories) on the inner ring, providing the finer-grained breakdown within the primary population. See the 1000 Genomes population descriptions for the reference panels and population definitions, and the HIGI Pipeline methods PDF for the full Stanford pipeline overview. [Needs confirmation from the Gloyn lab.] 3.12 Genetic Risk Scores Current coverage: 421 donors. Polygenic risk scores are computed from the same TOPMed-imputed genotypes described in the previous section. All scores undergo a static min-max normalization based on the theoretical minimum and maximum genetic-risk contributions (i.e. no risk alleles up to all risk alleles), mapping each raw PRS onto a 01 scale. The displayed risk is then expressed as a percentile against the current IIDP donor data freeze (e.g. Risk > 19% of IIDP donors), and for donors of European ancestry it is additionally expressed against the UK Biobank reference population (e.g. Risk > 25.27% of the European Population (UKBB)). The Stanford implementation lives at github.com/sethsh7/PRSedm (DOI:10.5281/zenodo.17903985); the full pipeline methods document is the HIGI Pipeline PDF. T1D Genetic Risk Score (T1D-GRS). Multiple published T1D-GRS variants are computed for each donor: t1dgrs2-luckett25  the 67-variant standardized score from Luckett et al. (2025, Diabetes Care, doi:10.2337/dc25-0142). t1dgrs2-qu22  the original GRS2 PRS with 4 additional African-ancestry SNPs (from Onengut) proposed by Qu et al. (2022, Pediatric Diabetes) and used in eMERGE. t1dgrs2-sharp21  the TOPMED-R2 version of GRS2 from Sharp et al. (2019, Diabetes Care, doi:10.2337/dc18-1785). Beyond the overall score, each donors T1D-GRS is decomposed into HLA Class 1, HLA Class 2, and Non-HLA contributions, and the donors DR3 / DR4 haplotype call is also reported (available via the IIDP Resource Data Repository). The trans-ancestry T1D-PRS is also downloadable from the RDR. T2D Genetic Risk Score (T2D-GRS). The genome-wide T2D-GRS is computed from the 1,232,226 variants of the multi-ancestry GWAS in Suzuki et al. (2024, Nature). Each donor is additionally given partitioned polygenic scores (pPS) that decompose their overall T2D risk into mechanistically distinct components, under a choice of two clustering frameworks: Soft clustering (Smith et al. 2024, Nature Medicine)  variants can contribute to multiple clusters with varying weights, allowing overlap and continuity across mechanisms. The clusters surfaced in the donor view include -cell dysfunction (two), obesity, lipodystrophy (two), proinsulin, bilirubin, cholesterol, liver lipid, hyperinsulin, SHBGi-LpA, and Alp-negative. Hard clustering (Suzuki et al. 2024, Nature)  each variant is uniquely assigned to a single cluster, representing relatively discrete genetic mechanisms. The clusters include residual glycemic, body fat, metabolic syndrome, obesity, -cell PI+, -cell PI, lipodystrophy, and liver-and-lipid metabolism. Both the ancestry and GRS pipelines are contributed by the lab of Dr. Anna Gloyn (Stanford); see the Contributors page. All data are released in versioned freezes: Version 2 is the current default (uses Suzuki 2024 for the T2D-GRS), while Version 1 is archived from the previous release (which used Mahajan et al. 2022 for the T2D-GRS and DiCorpo et al. 2022 for the partitioned scores). [Needs confirmation from the Gloyn lab.] 3.13 Pancreas Lipid Extraction Current coverage: 149 donors. Lipid extraction is performed on whole pancreas samples (not isolated islets) for a subset of donors, contributed by the lab of Dr. Erin Mulvihill (University of Ottawa). Data appear in the Donor View as a dedicated tab. The concentrations of triglyceride, total cholesterol, and free cholesterol in the pancreas were measured using enzyme-based assays. Lipids were extracted from approximately 100 mg of tissue using a modified Folch method involving chloroform and methanol. To account for procedural losses, samples were spiked with a radioactive recovery standard of ³H-Cholesterol Oleate (~100,000 dpm). Following extraction, lipid fractions were resolubilized with a fresh 1% Triton X-100 / chloroform solution to ensure proper reconstitution before the organic solvent was evaporated under nitrogen. The resulting dried lipids were resuspended in deionized water. Total Cholesterol (TC) was measured using Wako kit 439-17501 or Infinity Total Cholesterol reagents. Free Cholesterol (FC) was measured using Wako kit 435-35801. Triglycerides (TG) were measured using Roche kit #11877771216 or Infinity Triglyceride reagents. For triglyceride measurements, samples were further diluted using a 1% Triton/water dilution buffer to ensure results fell within the standard curve. Absorbance was read at 495 nm for triglycerides and 595 nm for cholesterol. Final values were corrected for recovery and normalized to the initial wet tissue weight, with results expressed as mg lipid per g wet tissue. Cholesteryl ester was calculated by the difference between total and free cholesterol. The standard curve for the Infinity reagents is prepared using a 200 g/mL lipid standard, creating a range from 0.25 to 8 g for both cholesterol and triolein. For 100 mg of tissue, typical aliquot volumes for the assay are 300500 L or up to 1 mL. After adding water to the dried Tritonlipid film, tubes are placed in a 37 °C shaking water bath for 15 minutes to ensure full suspension before the enzymatic assay. For the Infinity kit, the standard dilution factor is 75 (10 L of a 750 L sample). For WAKO/Roche kits, the dilution factors used in software calculations are 15 for cholesterol and 45 for triglycerides.

Chapter 4 Overview of Omics Data Types 4.1 Gene expression (bulk RNA-seq) Current coverage: 20,892 transcripts across 371 donors. On the day of sample collection, typically the shipment day (see section 3.5 above), 150 islets are hand picked and transferred to 1 ml of Trizol reagent. After vortexing, the sample is stored at -80°C until shipping or RNAseq at either Oxford or Stanford. At destination, RNA is extracted from Trizol as per manufacturer instructions and concentration and quality is assessed by NanoDrop. RNA integrity is further checked by Bioanalyzer (RNA 6000 chips) and 20 uL of RNA samples at 20 ng/uL minimum is submitted to Novogene for library prep and sequencing, on NovaSeq 6000 PE150 illumina platform, at 20M paired end reads per sample (6 G of raw data). After quality control via FastQC (v0.11.9), the raw reads were aligned to the human genome reference (GRCh38) using STAR (v2.7.9a) with the gene annotation downloaded from the ENSEMBL database (v110). Gene expression levels were counted using featureCounts (v2.0.3). Gene counts are processed for the web tool as follows. Genes are keyed by their Ensembl ID; Entrez ID, gene symbol, name and biotype are added as annotation and may be missing for some genes. Lowly expressed genes are removed with edgeRs filterByExpr (a minimum read count, scaled to library size, in a minimum share of donors). No variance filter is applied in the pre-processing step. Counts are normalized with the relative log expression (RLE) method and converted to log-counts-per-million (log-CPM). The data come from several sequencing batches, and all are kept: the batch effect is removed with ComBat on the log-CPM values, protecting Diabetes diagnosis so that its real effect is not removed with the batch. Only protein-coding and lncRNA genes are kept. The raw RNA sequencing data has been deposited in the European Genome-phenome Archive (EGA) under study number EGAS00001007241. 4.2 Gene expression (Nanostring) Current coverage: 156 transcripts across 259 donors. On the day of sample collection (see section 3.5, above) 50 islets are hand-picked at the ADI IsletCore, washed with PBS, then lysed in 100ul of RNeasy Lysis Buffer (RLT, Qiagen) containing 1% beta-mercaptoethanol. Samples are stored at -80oC before running on Nanostring gene expression assay at BC Children Hospital (Vancouver). The assay was updated partway through data collection, where a small number of genes were removed and replaced with others, resulting in different gene codesets. Briefly, 1ul cell lysate is used for hybridization with customized gene code sets that target 142 pancreatic islet genes and 6 reference genes. Hybridized complex is then loaded on cartridge and Nanostring nCounter to measure the target gene expression. The raw data is analyzed with nSolver4.0 software from Nanostring, producing a table of intensity values where larger values correspond to higher gene expression values. Full details are found here. Data Processing: Nanostring data come in three batches, which differ partly in the genes measured. Technical control probes (negative and positive spike-ins) are removed, and probes that were not run for a donor are set to missing. Intensities are normalized by sample median (each value divided by the median intensity of all genes for that donor) and log2-transformed. Batch effects are removed with ComBat, gene by gene across the batches that measured each gene; no biological variable is protected. Genes measured in only one batch cannot be corrected and are flagged so they are not compared across batches. Given the much smaller number of transcripts compared to the RNA-seq data, no abundance or variance filters are applied, and no donors are dropped. 4.3 Protein expression (proteomics) Current coverage: 234 donors in two batches  Batch 1: 8,546 proteins across 134 donors; Batch 2: 10,454 proteins across 100 donors; Combined: 8,338 proteins measured in both batches. Human islets are shipped to the University of British Columbia, hand-picked and cultured in RPMI for 24-72hrs before the experiment to allow the islets to recover from shipping. After recovery, 300 islets are hand-picked, washed with PBS and the pellet is snap frozen and stored at -80oC. LC-MS/MS analysis is performed with n = 3 technical replicates, using a NanoElute UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics) with Aurora Series Gen2 (CSI) analytical column coupled to a Trapped Ion Mobility  Time of Flight mass spectrometer (timsTOF Pro; Bruker Daltonics, Germany) operated in Data-Independent Acquisition - Parallel Accumulation- Serial Fragmentation (DIA-PASEF) mode. Details of lysis and analysis are found in Kolic et al. (2024) Cell Metabolism. Proteomics data come in two batches acquired at different times: Batch 1 (three technical runs per donor) and Batch 2 (later donors). Protein intensities come from DIA-NN. Each batch is processed the same way: intensities are log2-transformed and normalized with cyclic loess (limma), repeat runs of a donor are averaged after normalization, and proteins detected in too few of the batchs donors are removed. Missing values are then filled with limpas exponential tilting method (Li & Smyth 2023), using each batchs own detection curve; measured values are not changed. The two batches are also combined, keeping the proteins that pass in each batch, with no variance filter. Because the batches differ systematically, the combined data can be used in two ways: Batch corrected, where the batch effect is removed with ComBat while protecting Diabetes diagnosis (Type 2 vs No Diabetes), or Batch as covariate, where the uncorrected data are used and batch is added to the model automatically. Multi-omics integration (chapter 5) uses the ComBat-corrected data. Raw proteomics data has been deposited to ProteomExchange via MASSive under dataset number PXD045422. [The sample preparation and LC-MS/MS description above and dataset PXD045422 are from v1 (Batch 1); the v2 (Batch 2) protocol and data deposition need confirmation from the Johnson lab.] 4.4 Gene expression (pseudobulk RNA-seq) Current coverage: 58 HumanIslets donors with pseudobulk profiles. The single-cell counts from patch-seq data (section 4.5, below) were summarized at the donor by separating counts by cell type (alpha and beta). Only cells from donors with at least five cells were retained. Pseudobulk profiles were created by summing counts from all cells derived from the same donor. Ensembl gene IDs were mapped to Entrez IDs and counts from any duplicated Entrez IDs were summed. Each matrix was filtered to remove transcripts with greater than 80% zeros. Counts were converted to logCPM values using the TMM method from the edgeR R package (version 3.38.4). Due to the large variations in sequencing depth across batches, individual transcripts that had zero or one count were replaced with NA values. 4.5 Single-cell gene expression (patch-seq) Current coverage: 61 HumanIslets donors with patch-seq cells. The collection and analysis of pancreas patch-seq data is described here and here. Reads from FASTQ files were trimmed using TrimGalore version 0.6.5 with auto-detection of adapter sequence, then aligned and counted using STAR version 2.7.9a to the GRCh38 human genome (Ensembl release 104). Cell count matrices were loaded into R and a Seurat object was generated using the Seurat R package (version 4.3.0). Only cells with patch-clamp data were included; data for additional cells are available from the listed accession numbers below. Cell types were identified by projection, using the MapQuery command from the R package Seurat, onto a large set of human islet single cell RNAseq data generated from publicly available data (see below). Cells were filtered to remove any that were not alpha or beta cells, had fewer than 500 total counts across all transcripts, had fewer than 300 unique transcripts with non-zero count values, or had greater than 20% mitochondrial DNA. Ensembl gene IDs were mapped to Entrez IDs and counts from any duplicated Entrez IDs were summed. Counts were separated by cell type (alpha and beta) and glucose concentration (1, 5, and 10mM), resulting in six different matrices. Each matrix was filtered to remove transcripts with greater than 80% zeros. Counts were converted to logCPM values using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method from the edgeR R package (version 3.38.4). TMM has been shown to perform better for single-cell RNAseq data compared to the RLE method because it is robust to the high drop-out rate. Individual transcripts that had zero counts were replaced with NA. Raw sequencing reads are available in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under accession numbers GSE124742 and GSE164875 and GSE270484 at PancDB (https://hpap.pmacs.upenn.edu/). 4.6 Single-cell RNA-seq Reads from FASTQ files were trimmed using TrimGalore version 0.6.5 with auto-detection of adapter sequence, then aligned to the GRCh38 human genome, Ensembl release 104, and counted using STAR version 2.7.9a except for files from GSE84133, which were aligned and counted using the inDrops protocol; files from GSE81076 and GSE85241, which were aligned and counted using the R package scruff (version 1.10.1) with Rsubread (version 1.22.2); and files from GSE269204, which were aligned and counted with Cell Ranger (10X Genomics Cell Ranger v6.1.2). Cell count matrices were loaded into R and objects generated using the R package Seurat (version 4.3.0), restricted to transcripts detected in more than 10 cells and cells with between 200 and 12,500 unique transcripts with non-zero count values; cells with percent mitochondrial transcripts in the top 25% for each dataset were also dropped. Transcript names were maintained as Ensembl identifiers to preserve the greatest number of unique transcripts. After combining all donors, transcripts expressed in fewer than 0.1% of cells were filtered. Donor HPAP-027 was dropped from the data set because there were very few cells (32 cells). The reciprocal PCA integration with references (HPAP-037, HPAP-040; HPAP-045, HPAP-050, HPAP-052, and HPAP-072) workflow from the R package Seurat (version 4.3.0) was followed, with k.anchor = 5, then FindNeighbors and FindCluster (resolution = 1.2). Cell types were first manually annotated based on the unambiguous, high level expression of marker genes in distinct clusters in UMAP space, except cytotoxic T cells, which did not form a distinct cluster but had restricted expression of TRAC. The remaining ambiguous cells were annotated using the MapQuery function by projecting unknown cells onto the manually annotated cells. Although these data include cells from donors with type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes, only cells from donors with no diabetes (ND) are visualised in the web tool for cell-type localization of called features, and are not downloadable. Data are from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under accession numbers GSE81076, GSE81547, GSE81608, GSE83139, GSE84133, GSE85241, GSE86469, GSE154126; from the European Molecular Biology Laboratory European Biology Institute (EMBL-EBI) under accession number E-MTAB-5061; from the Human Pancreas Analysis Program at PancDB up to donor HPAP-109, and from unpublished data (GSE269204). 4.7 Metabolomics Current coverage: 215 annotated metabolite features across 38 donors (38 at low glucose, 37 at high glucose and in ratio form), measured at low (2.8 mM) and high (16.7 mM) glucose, with ratio also reported. Metabolomics samples are collected on islets handled at the ADI IsletCore under the same two glucose conditions used elsewhere in the platform  low glucose (LG, 2.8 mM) and high glucose (HG, 16.7 mM)  so that metabolite intensities can be compared at fasting-like versus stimulation-like conditions and an HG/LG ratio can be reported alongside each absolute value. Samples are analysed by liquid chromatographymass spectrometry. Raw mzML spectra are acquired across two batches (B1 and B2) in both positive- and negative-ion modes. Peak picking is performed with Asari (xialabs open-source MS preprocessor), producing per-mode preferred feature tables and a feature-level annotation file. Feature tables are then processed in MetaboAnalyst (xialabs metabolomics platform; see https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/). Post-processing of the MetaboAnalyst output is implemented in a custom R pipeline: Blank filtering: features that are not appreciably elevated over process blanks are dropped. Detection (QC) filtering: features whose intensity is unstable across pooled QC injections are dropped. Normalization: median normalisation (each sample divided by its median feature intensity) followed by log transform. Batch correction: the production pipeline uses ComBat (parametric empirical Bayes, sva R package), with donor diabetes status included as a protected covariate so the inter-batch correction preserves biological T2D-versus-no-diabetes signal. Three alternatives were benchmarked during method selection  WaveICA 2.0 (wavelet + ICA, no batch labels required), QC-RLSC (QC-based LOESS signal correction), and median-only  and ComBat-with-diagnosis was selected on the basis of PCA separation and downstream replicability. MS2 annotation: once corrected, the feature tables are merged with MS2-level annotations (HMDB IDs, main class, sub class) to produce the final 215 annotated metabolites surfaced in the platform. Positive- and negative-mode results are combined into a single donor × metabolite matrix at low glucose, high glucose, and as the HG/LG log-ratio. 4.8 Environmental Contaminants Current coverage: 58 contaminant measurements across 31 donors. Environmental contaminants were quantified in pancreas and adipose tissue samples by the lab of Dr. Jenny Bruin (Carleton University). For each donor, multiple ~5 mm cubic biopsies of pancreas and peripancreatic adipose tissue were collected and flash frozen. The frozen tissue biopsies were sent to SGS AXYS (Sidney, BC, Canada) to measure a panel of 17 dioxin/furan, 16 PCB, and 28 OCP analytes using GC-MS/MS; SGS AXYS is ISO 17025 accredited by the Canadian Association for Laboratory Accreditation. Sample concentrations were determined based on labelled surrogate standard quantification and sample weight, and were adjusted for percent recovery. Sample limits of detection (LOD) were established based on a 3:1 signal-to-background-noise ratio. Analytes that had NDR flags (defined by SGS AXYS as a peak that was detected but did not meet quantification criteria) in more than 40% of donors were excluded from the dataset. This included 2 dioxin/furans in adipose, 1 dioxin/furan in pancreas, and 2 OCPs in both adipose and pancreas, leaving a total of 57 and 58 analytes in adipose and pancreas, respectively. Analytes that passed the NDR inclusion criteria were blank-adjusted using batch-specific lab blank values (labelled Blank adjusted on the web tool). Data are also provided as Blank and LOD adjusted: for these data, if a donor had a non-detect (ND) flag for an analyte that met the NDR criteria, it was assigned a value equivalent to half the batch-specific LOD for that analyte. In addition to individual analyte concentrations, arithmetic sums are provided for dioxins/furans and PCBs. For PCBs, the sums of dioxin-like (DL) PCBs, non-dioxin-like (NDL) PCBs, and all PCBs are provided. Because contaminant data are typically zero-inflated and non-normal, in-tool analyses use Kendall rank correlation (partial Kendall when covariates are supplied) rather than the moderated-t approach used for transcriptomics/proteomics; see chapter 5 (Kendall rank correlation) for details. The detailed measurement and quality-control protocol is described in Hoyeck et al. (2026) Nature Communications, doi:10.1038/s41467-026-71847-5. The first cohort for contaminant analysis includes 14 females and 17 males, with ages ranging from 2570, BMI ranging from 12.840.3, and HbA1c ranging from 3.68.6%. Of the 31 donors, 4 were clinically diagnosed with T2D and 1 had an HbA1c in the pre-T2D range. This cohort is described in detail in Hoyeck et al. (2026) Nature Communications, doi:10.1038/s41467-026-71847-5. Additional environmental contaminant data on a larger cohort of donors are forthcoming. 4.9 DNA Methylation Current coverage: 729,123 CpG sites across 50 donors (Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC v2.0 array). Genome-wide DNA methylation is profiled on the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC v2.0 (EPICv2) BeadChip, contributed by our collaborators in Singapore. Raw -values (the methylated fraction at each probe, 01) are reported for 784,789 probes per donor and processed into the platforms analysis tables through a custom R pipeline: Probe filtering: only cg (CpG) probes are kept (control, SNP and non-CpG probes are dropped) and sex-chromosome probes are removed; the sesame recommended EPICv2 mask (all-ancestry union at 1% minor-allele frequency) is then applied to drop poor-mapping, cross-reactive and polymorphic probes, leaving 729,123 CpG sites. Replicate collapse: EPICv2 carries several replicate probes per CpG; these are averaged to a single value per CpG.  and M values: both scales are stored   (01, used for interpretation and display) and M = log2( / (1  )), the variance-stabilised scale used for statistical testing. Annotation: each CpG is annotated on hg38 using the Bioconductor EPICv2 annotation: genomic coordinate, UCSC RefGene gene and gene region, and CpG-island relation (Island / Shore / Shelf / OpenSea). As is typical for EPIC arrays, roughly one third of CpGs fall within a RefGene gene and the remainder lie in intergenic / open-sea regions. 4.10 Metabolic Flux Current coverage: 2,771 reactions at high glucose (2,775 at low glucose; 2,765 in ratio form) across 371 donors. Donor-specific genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) are built from the Human-GEM v1.19.0 reconstruction and loaded into COBRApy from per-donor MATLAB-format model files. ATP hydrolysis (Human-GEM reaction MAR03964) is set as the cellular objective. The platform simulates two glucose conditions and two media compositions: Low glucose (LG): approximately 2.8 mM (the glucose exchange reaction is bounded at 2.0 flux units, matching the GSIS / perifusion / metabolomics LG condition). High glucose (HG): approximately 16.7 mM (glucose exchange bounded at 10.0 flux units, matching the platforms HG stimulation condition). Both conditions are simulated under glucose-only media and under glucose plus amino-acid supplementation (with fixed uptake rates for glutamine, alanine, serine, etc.); the amino-acid scenario opens alternative carbon entry into the TCA cycle. For each donor × condition, Flux Variability Analysis (FVA) is run on the entire reaction network at a 90% optimality fraction; the platform stores the FVA minimum, maximum, centre, and span per reaction. OptGP flux sampling (5,000 samples, thinning = 100) is run on top of FVA to capture the achievable flux distribution; from the samples the pipeline records the mean, median, standard deviation, and 25/75% quartiles per reaction. Per-reaction flux values are signed-log2 transformed and z-scored within each donor before being loaded into the analysis tables so the downstream limma model sees comparable distributions across reactions. The HG/LG ratio table stores the per-reaction log-ratio between high glucose and low glucose conditions, capturing each donors glucose responsiveness at the flux level.
