Chapter 5 Overview of statistical analysis methods 5.1 Multiple linear regression Linear models are used to compute omics featuremetadata associations for the Bulk gene expression (RNA-seq), Bulk gene expression (Nanostring), Bulk protein expression, Pseudobulk gene expression, Metabolite intensity, DNA Methylation (on M-values) and Metabolic flux simulation datasets. Single-cell gene expression (patch-seq) and Environmental contaminants use rank correlation instead (sections 5.2 and 5.3). A linear model containing the selected metadata variable of interest and all covariates (if any) is fit to the expression or abundance levels of each feature in the selected omics dataset, using the limma R package. If the user selects a categorical metadata of interest, two dropdowns automatically appear so that a specific contrast can be specified (ie. type 2 diabetes versus no diabetes). Then, the coefficient of the metadata variable (continuous) or metadata contrast (categorical) of interest and its associated p-value are extracted from the model for each feature. P-values are adjusted using the false discovery rate method. The rationale for using the original limma method is that it has been shown to perform well for many omics types as long as the data are appropriately normalized and transformed. While more customized methods developed for specific omics types may perform slightly better when applied to the appropriate data type, the advantage of our approach is that it can be applied to many omics types without modification, making the results more comparable to each other and making the HumanIslets tool easier to maintain. A detailed explanation of how analyze omics data with multiple linear regression, including how to specify linear models for different research questions and how to interpret the results, is available in Protocol #2 here. 5.1.1 Wilcoxon rank-sum check For a two-group comparison without covariates, the Omics View also runs a Wilcoxon rank-sum test on the same features and donors used by limma, as a check that does not rely on normally distributed data. The effect size is the AUC: the probability that a donor from one group has a higher value than a donor from the other. It is computed with the presto R package; features with missing values are tested on their own non-missing donors with base Rs wilcox.test, using the normal approximation with continuity correction. P-values are adjusted with the false discovery rate over the same features as limma. The test is not run for DNA methylation, when covariates are selected (the Wilcoxon test cannot adjust for them, and this includes an automatically added batch covariate), or when either group has too few donors. 5.2 Spearman ranked correlation Due to the highly nonlinear nature of the relationships between single-cell gene expression and single-cell electrophysiology outcomes (patch-seq), Spearman correlation (base R) is used to compute feature-metadata relationships for the patchSeq data. Only single-cell electrophysiology outcomes are available for analysis with the single-cell expression data, and covariate adjustment is not supported. For these analyses, electrophysiology parameters other than the half-inactivation sodium current were normalized to cell size. The sign of the calcium entry, sodium current, and calcium current (early and late) electrophysiology parameters was flipped such that greater values correspond to greater currents. Negative exocytosis values were replaced with zeros. 5.3 Kendall rank correlation (environmental contaminants) Environmental contaminant abundances are typically zero-inflated and non-normal, which violates the distributional assumptions used by moderated-t (limma) for the other omics types. For contaminants, the platform therefore substitutes Kendalls rank correlation, which is a non-parametric alternative that is better suited to the current sample size (n = 31). When no covariates are selected, contaminantphenotype associations are computed with base Rs cor.test(..., method = "kendall"); when covariates are supplied, the same test is run as a partial correlation using ppcor::pcor.test(..., method = "kendall"). Both continuous and dichotomized (0/1) contrasts of the analysis variable are supported. The reported coefficient is Kendalls tau (not a log-fold-change), and the same BenjaminiHochberg FDR adjustment is applied to the resulting p-values. 5.4 Pathway analysis Overrepresentation analysis (ORA) and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) are supported for pathway analysis of the feature association results. Both methods are implemented using the fgsea R package. The feature list used for ORA is determined by the p-value threshold specified in the association analysis. GSEA can be performed using either the model coefficient (or log2FC when the metadata is categorical) or the test statistic from the association analysis to rank the features. For the patch-seq data, the coefficient is the correlation estimate and there is no test statistic option as it is not compatible with the Spearman correlation results. There are six supported pathway libraries, including KEGG, Reactome, the full Gene Ontology term list (broken into Biological Process, Cellular Component, and Molecular Function), and the PANTHER summary of the Gene Ontology terms (also broken into the same three categories). Pathway analysis can sometimes return a high number of significant pathways or gene sets that consist of mostly the same features, leading to a redundant results list. Users have the option of collapsing redundant sets, which uses the collapsePathways function within the fgsea R package to filter the gene sets to only include those with independent gene lists. Pathway analysis is not supported for the Nanostring data, as there are too few features (n = 156) for adequate pathway coverage. 5.5 Pre-computed feature associations Two complementary families of associations are pre-computed: univariate associations (one feature at a time) and multivariate predictions (one omics matrix against a target, jointly). Univariate associations are shown in the Feature View and IsletAgent; multivariate predictions are shown in IsletAgent. 5.5.1 Univariate associations Univariate associations were computed between all omics feature-metadata variable pairs and between all metadata variable-metadata variable pairs. The linear model and Spearman correlation methods described above were used to compute the omics-metadata associations, with one modification. Some categorical variables have obvious specific contrasts, for example for diabetes status, one is usually interested in type 1 versus no diabetes and type 2 versus no diabetes. In these cases, we specify each contrast of interest using the methods described above. Other variables do not have obvious comparisons, for example donation type, so in this case an ANOVA style analysis is done and the statistics are extracted for the categorical variable coefficient rather than for a specific contrast. Sex, age, BMI, and culture time were included as covariates for analyses that used a linear model (all bulk omics data associations). Three different methods were used to compute associations between pairs of metadata, depending on whether each metadata in the pair were continuous or categorical. Pearson correlation was used for continuous-continuous pairs, Cramers V correlation was used for categorical-categorical pairs, and ANOVA was used for categorical-continuous pairs where the categorical variable is the independent variable and the continuous variable is the dependent variable. Multiple hypothesis correction (FDR method) was performed across all results for the same statistical method. Some metadata variables such as percent purity and percent trapped are in between ordinal variables and a true continuous variable because they are estimates made by eye by a research technician, and the technician tends to estimate whole percentages (ie. 80%, 70%). For simplicity, we treat these as continuous variables. 5.5.2 Multivariate predictions In addition to the univariate results, the platform pre-computes multivariate prediction models for each (omics matrix × target phenotype) combination. Where univariate analysis tests each feature in isolation, the multivariate models fit all features in an omics jointly to a target, capturing the predictive signal that distributes across many features. Six complementary methods are run per omics × target so that linear and non-linear signal are both surfaced: Method Use case Notes Elastic Net (cross-validated) Continuous targets Linear, sparse feature selection Logistic Elastic Net (cross-validated) Binary pairwise contrasts Linear classifier with sparse selection Multinomial Elastic Net (cross-validated) Discrete targets with  3 levels Linear, multi-class Stability Selection Any Lasso / Logistic-Lasso refit over 100 random subsamples; selection frequency indicates feature robustness Random Forest + permutation importance Any Non-linear; importance magnitude only (no signed direction) XGBoost + SHAP Any Non-linear with per-feature signed direction from SHAP values; GPU-accelerated when available Only models whose cross-validated quality passes a minimum (R² for continuous targets, AUC for binary targets) are kept and shown. The results feed the Prediction panel in IsletAgent. 5.6 Deconvolution analysis Cell type proportions are estimated from the bulk proteomics data (both batches). After normalization, the level of a marker protein that is abundant in only one cell type, and fairly constant within it, is proportional to the amount of that cell type. Marker proteins for , ,  and  cells come from a reference marker list; a protein group is used only if it marks exactly one cell type. A marker is kept only if it follows the core markers of its cell type across donors (Spearman r  0.3; core markers such as INS, GCG, SST and PPY are always kept, and all -cell markers are kept). Only measured values are used (filled-in values are set back to missing), and each marker is compared with its median within the donors own batch, so the two proteomics batches can be combined without batch correction. We assume an average of 0.55  cells, 0.30  cells, 0.10  cells and 0.05  cells; each cell types estimate is this prior times the median fold change of its markers, so the values are relative and the median donor sits on these averages. The endocrine proportions are then expressed as shares of the endocrine total, so they add up to 1. The non-endocrine proportion is 1  0.98 × (endocrine total / the highest donors endocrine total), assuming the most endocrine-rich donor is 98% endocrine. It is a separate variable, Non-endocrine cell proportion (computed), which can be added as a covariate in the Omics View. Overall, this can be thought of as estimating the strength of the signal associated with four endocrine cell types, anchoring the median signal strength with prior known cell type proportions, and attributing any missing signal to trapped non-endocrine cells. It relies on the assumptions that marker genes are only expressed in one cell type and that their levels are constant across donors. Neither of these assumptions are completely satisfied, however the method should be a robust estimator so long as the majority of marker genes have heavily biased expression in one cell type and if all marker genes are not regulated in the same direction (ie. all beta cell marker genes up-regulated in donors with diabetes). 5.7 Multi-omics integration methods WGCNA and MOFA are precomputed for each supported combination of omics types; DIABLO runs when you submit. All three use only the donors measured in every selected omics type. WGCNA and MOFA need at least 20 such donors (for MOFA, every pair of omics types must also share 20), and DIABLO needs at least 10 with a value for the outcome. Large omics matrices are reduced to their most variable features before integration, so no single omics type dominates. For integration, RNA-seq is variance-stabilized (DESeq2 vst) and ComBat batch-corrected, and proteomics and metabolomics enter already ComBat batch-corrected. Results can be limited to a donor subset; for WGCNA and MOFA, the modules and factors stay as precomputed and the phenotype associations are recalculated for the chosen donors. See chapter 2 (Multi-omics View) for how to use these methods. 5.7.1 WGCNA (Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis) Each omics matrix is z-scored, reduced to its most variable features (median absolute deviation), and joined into one matrix, with the omics type added to each feature ID. One network is built on the joined matrix, so a module can hold features from more than one omics type. Combinations cover RNA-seq, proteomics, Nanostring, pseudobulk, metabolic flux and DNA methylation. Feature caps are smaller when three omics types are combined, to keep the network manageable. Correlation uses biweight midcorrelation (bicor). The network is signed hybrid with a signed topological overlap (TOM). The soft-threshold power is the lowest that gives a good scale-free fit, with a minimum for signed networks. Module size, merge height and deepSplit adapt to the number of donors and features. Module eigengenes come from WGCNA::moduleEigengenes(). Each feature has its signed module membership (kME) and intramodular connectivity, and the strongest TOM edges of each module are kept for the network view. Modulephenotype associations use Pearson correlation for continuous and binary phenotypes and ANOVA (effect size) for multi-level categorical phenotypes, with BenjaminiHochberg adjustment within each module and test type. Pathway enrichment for a module (ORA, or GSEA ranked by kME) runs on request. 5.7.2 MOFA (Multi-Omics Factor Analysis) MOFA is computed with the MOFA2 R package on the donors measured in every omics type of the combination. Large omics matrices are reduced to their most variable features (median absolute deviation); annotated metabolites, metabolic flux and Nanostring are kept whole. Features are z-scored. The number of factors is set from the number of shared donors, up to a maximum. All views use a Gaussian likelihood, views and groups are not rescaled (the data are already scaled), training converges more slowly for small cohorts, and a fixed random seed is used. Precomputed outputs include donor factor scores, feature loadings per omics, and the variance explained per factor and omics. Factorphenotype associations use the same tests as WGCNA. The Circos Plot shows the top-loading features of a factor in each omics, linked by their Pearson correlation across shared donors. Pathway enrichment for a factor runs on request. 5.7.3 DIABLO (Data Integration Analysis for Biomarker discovery using Latent cOmponents) DIABLO is a supervised integration that runs when you submit, using the mixOmics R package and a primary metadata variable as the outcome. A two-group outcome uses block.splsda; a continuous outcome uses block.pls in regression mode. Each group needs a minimum number of donors. If covariates are selected, they are regressed out of each omics block (limma removeBatchEffect) while the outcome is kept. Each block is then screened with limma, keeping the features most associated with the outcome (DNA methylation is first reduced by variance), and z-scored. Blocks are linked by a fixed design weight, and DIABLO selects a small, fixed number of features per block and component; there is no cross-validation tuning, so the page stays fast. No AUROC is shown, because a score computed on the same donors used to fit the model would be over-optimistic. The signed limma statistics from the screen rank features for GSEA in the pathway analysis. 5.8 Variational Autoencoder (VAE) for donor clustering The Cluster View groups donors by their islet molecular profiles, without using clinical labels. The clustering uses bulk RNA-seq and proteomics, the two omics layers measured in the most donors. Patch-seq and metabolomics are measured in fewer donors, so they are left out to avoid selection bias. Input data: Each omics layer contributes its most variable features. A curated set of islet genes is always kept, whatever its rank (-cell identity and function, MODY and diabetes risk genes, islet stress and apoptosis, exocytosis and ion channels). Marker genes of contaminating cell types are removed. Removal of technical variation: Each feature is adjusted for isolation variables: Purity (%), Trapped (%), Cold Ischemic Time (h), Digestion time (min), Collagenase supplier, Collagenase type and Donation Type. RNA-seq is also adjusted for Culture time (h) and Total islet equivalents (IEQ). Features are also adjusted for acinar and ductal marker scores. BMI, HbA1c (%), genetic ancestry and Diabetes diagnosis are protected, so only technical variation is removed. Age and sex are neither protected nor removed. Each layer is then converted to z-scores. Model: A multi-view VAE with product-of-experts (PoE) fusion learns one shared summary (the latent space) for each donor. Each omics layer has its own encoder and decoder. PoE combines the layers by their precision, so a donor measured in only one layer is kept without imputing the other layer. The loss is the reconstruction error plus a KullbackLeibler (KL) term. The KL weight starts at zero, rises slowly and stays small, which keeps more latent dimensions active. Training uses the Adam optimizer with weight decay and early stopping. No phenotype is used to train the VAE. Reading the latent space: Repeated training gives different latent spaces, and clusters formed directly on the latent coordinates were not reproducible. The model is therefore trained many times with different random seeds. In each run, ridge regression with cross-validation predicts each clinical and functional phenotype from the latent space, so each donors score comes from a model that never saw that donors value. Technical variables, proteomics-derived cell composition and sex are not used. A phenotype is kept when its predictions match the measured values (Spearman correlation, FDR-controlled) in at least half of the runs. Closely related phenotypes are combined into a small set of phenotype directions. These directions are read-outs of the latent space and add no new information, but unlike the latent coordinates, they are reproducible across runs. Clustering: Donors are grouped by k-means on their direction scores. Each donors scores come from its own omics data, through models that never saw that donors phenotypes. So a donors cluster reflects its omics profile, not its own phenotypes. The number of clusters was chosen by agreement across random half-splits of the training runs, the size of the smallest cluster, and the phenotype differences between clusters. Donors without omics data: Donors without RNA-seq or proteomics are assigned to a cluster from their phenotypes, by multinomial logistic regression trained on the omics donors. A separate model is fitted for each pattern of available measurements: clinical data (Age, Sex, BMI, HbA1c (%) and Diabetes diagnosis), static insulin secretion, insulin content, pancreas lipids and Seahorse respiration. Each model uses only the measurements a donor has, so nothing is imputed. Each assignment comes with the probability of the assigned cluster and a reliability level: high, medium or low. Predicted clusters are a guide for each donor. Cluster statistics use omics donors, or omics donors plus high-reliability predicted donors where stated. Cluster characterization: Each cluster is compared with all other clusters combined. Continuous phenotypes are tested with Welchs t test (effect size: Cohens d), and categorical phenotypes with the ² test (effect size: Cramérs V). Omics features are compared among omics donors with limma, without covariates. Pathways are tested by pre-ranked enrichment (fgsea) of the limma t statistics against KEGG, Reactome and Gene Ontology Molecular Function gene sets (KEGG only for metabolites). P-values are adjusted with the BenjaminiHochberg false discovery rate (FDR). Comparisons can use omics donors only, or also add predicted donors at high, high-or-medium, or any reliability. 5.9 GEM Library for Pathway Enrichment Pathway analysis in HumanIslets supports three GEM-based libraries in addition to the standard KEGG / Reactome / Gene Ontology / PANTHER options, selectable from the same library dropdown used for the standard pathway libraries: KEGG human metabolite-centred pathways: KEGG pathways organised around the participating metabolites rather than the catalysing enzymes. Human1 GEM reactions grouped by participating metabolite: useful when ranking metabolite-feature association results into the broader metabolic context. Human1 GEM reactions grouped by metabolic subsystem (e.g., glycolysis, TCA cycle, amino-acid metabolism): the most commonly used GEM library when ranking flux-feature association results. The same fgsea::fora() (ORA) and fgsea::fgsea() (GSEA) implementations described above are used; the only thing that changes is which annotation object the library is loaded from. Path-collapse (redundancy removal) is also supported via the corresponding fgsea::collapsePathways() / collapsePathwaysORA() helpers, so users can collapse highly overlapping reaction sets when the resulting hit list is long. 5.10 Sources of gene annotations & link to code repository Gene annotation is matched by Ensembl gene ID: Entrez IDs, gene symbols, descriptions and biotypes come from Ensembl BioMart, Bioconductor org.Hs.eg.db and g:Profiler, with symbols checked against HGNC (built February 2026). Protein groups keep the gene names reported by DIA-NN, and their Entrez IDs are matched by gene symbol. Copies of all associated R scripts, including functions called by the HumanIslets tool, scripts used for data processing and analysis, and scripts for generating manuscript figures are available at this repository.

Chapter 6 GIFT Genomic View The GIFT Genomic View (section 2.3.2) shows islet genetic results from GIFT, a resource led by the Gloyn lab, which provides all genetic data in HumanIslets. The Gloyn lab produced these associations; HumanIslets stores them and draws the plots and tables. This chapter describes what the view holds, how the page builds its plots, and the quick colocalisation test. [GIFT citation and data-use terms to be added; needs confirmation from the Gloyn lab.] 6.1 Data in the view Current coverage: 519 genotyped donors and 7,764,556 variants. Islet function GWAS (GWAS-in-a-dish): genome-wide associations between genetic variants and donor islet phenotypes, for example Static-secretion stimulation index. 50 phenotypes in five groups: Static GSIS: 6 phenotypes, 377 donors; Bayesian hierarchical model: 25 phenotypes, 376 donors; Dynamic perifusion: 6 phenotypes, 148 donors; Beta-cell electrophysiology: 6 phenotypes, 300 donors; Alpha-cell electrophysiology: 7 phenotypes, 88 donors. Islet cis-QTLs: variants linked to a nearby molecular feature: eQTL (gene expression), exon-level eQTL (exon expression), sQTL (splicing junction), pQTL (protein) and caQTL (chromatin peak). eQTL: 12,826 significant lead signals, mapped in 954 donors (448 GIFT donors and 506 donors from published islet RNA-seq studies: CRG, InsPIRE, TIGER and van de Bunt et al.); caQTL: 5,159 lead signals in 139 donors; pQTL: 567 lead signals in 113 donors. Covariate models: each GWAS phenotype has three models: primary, T2D-adjusted and BMI-adjusted. Some static insulin secretion phenotypes use content-adjusted versions of the same three models (labelled content-adj.). The primary model is shown first. Positions and alleles: variant positions use GRCh38 (hg38). In GWAS tables the effect size is per copy of the effect allele; in QTL tables it is per copy of the ALT allele. 6.2 How the plots are built Significance lines: plots mark genome-wide significance (P = 5×10-8, dashed red) and the suggestive level (P = 10-5, dotted grey). Manhattan plot: every variant with P < 0.05 is drawn as it is; the rest are downsampled so the plot loads quickly. The table below lists the top 1,000 variants by P. Locus plot: all QTL hits in the genes cis window, one colour per QTL type. The lead variant of each feature is drawn as a diamond. Function GWAS: for each islet function trait, the strongest GWAS variant in the genes cis window and its distance from the QTL lead variant. Regional plot: all GWAS variants within ±500 kb of the selected variant, for one phenotype and model. 6.3 Colocalisation Colocalisation asks whether two association signals in one region share a causal variant. The coloc method gives five probabilities that add up to 1: PP.H0: neither trait is associated in the region; PP.H1: only the first trait is associated; PP.H2: only the second trait is associated; PP.H3: both are associated, with two different causal variants; PP.H4: both are associated, with one shared causal variant. Results from the GIFT paper. When a gene is in the GIFT colocalisation results, the tab shows them. The locus plot for each pair is drawn from the current summary statistics on this site, so P values can differ a little from the GIFT results. Quick test. When a gene is not in those results, a Quick test can be run for reference. It tests the genes cis-QTL (one QTL type at a time) against every islet function GWAS phenotype, using the current summary statistics. It uses the coloc approximate Bayes factor method (coloc.abf() in the R coloc package): default coloc priors: p1 = p2 = 1×10-4, p12 = 1×10-5; variants with minor allele frequency > 5%; alleles aligned, with mismatched and strand-ambiguous (A/T, C/G) variants removed; a ±250 kb window around the lead variant, and one QTL feature per gene (the one with the strongest lead); a sensitivity check: the share of p12 values from 10-8 to 10-4 that still give PP.H4 > 0.5. Results are sorted by PP.H4, and every result is shown. The Quick test uses no LD reference panel, so it cannot separate several independent signals at one locus. Chapter 7 IsletAgent IsletAgent (section 2.3.1) works on a knowledge graph that holds the HumanIslets cohort results and public evidence in one structure. This chapter describes what is in the knowledge graph, how IsletAgent uses it, and how the evidence for each relationship is graded. 7.1 Architecture overview IsletAgent page (Angular frontend)  question  IsletAgent (fine-tuned small language model, run locally)  retrieval call  reviewed query templates (Cypher)  Neo4j knowledge graph  analysis call  cohort analyses (platform API)   Evidence-graded answer: verdict, panels, tables, methods and R scripts The knowledge graph is stored in Neo4j. IsletAgent does not write free-form database queries. It names the entities, the retrieval route and a few parameters, and a reviewed query template writes the Cypher. So every knowledge graph query is valid and can be inspected. When a question needs a calculation that is not stored in the knowledge graph, IsletAgent calls one of the platforms analyses, and the platform runs it on the cohort data. 7.2 Knowledge graph The knowledge graph is built in five layers, so each kind of evidence can be updated on its own. 7.2.1 Public knowledge PrimeKG, Hetionet and public pathway resources. This layer covers diabetes-related diseases, genes, drugs and their indications, environmental exposures, tissue expression in the pancreas and islets, Gene Ontology processes, proteinprotein and gene-regulatory interactions, pathways and drugtarget links. This layer holds islet cis-eQTLs and cis-pQTLs, which give the main genetic support for causal analyses, together with exon-level eQTLs, splicing QTLs (sQTLs), chromatin-accessibility QTLs (caQTLs) and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of islet phenotypes. A cis-QTL is called significant after Bonferroni correction across the variants tested for each feature and BenjaminiHochberg correction across features. 7.2.5 Local data The HumanIslets cohort itself: donors, their phenotype values, and pre-computed links between molecular features and donor phenotypes. Associations come from limma linear models adjusted for age, sex, BMI and culture time (Kendall partial correlation for contaminants, Spearman correlation for patch-seq). Prediction links show how well each omics layer predicts each phenotype (elastic net, stability selection, random forest, and XGBoost with SHAP). Only models above a quality floor are kept. 7.3 How IsletAgent works Model: IsletAgent is a small, instruction-tuned language model. It is fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation on a quantized model (QLoRA), using grounded examples from the knowledge graph, and runs privately on local hardware. Tasks: it is trained on three tasks that follow the agent workflow: Parsing: resolve the entities in a question, expand concepts into their measurements, and choose the retrieval route. Grounded reasoning: turn the retrieved evidence into one evidence-based answer. Analysis: decide whether to run a cohort analysis or stop when the evidence is enough. Retrieval and analysis: for retrieval, IsletAgent sends a call naming the entities, the route and its parameters, and a reviewed template writes the Cypher. For computation, it calls one of the platforms analyses: feature characterization, donor-group comparisons, differential expression, phenotype association, pathway enrichment, colocalization, Mendelian randomization and QTL look-ups in the cohorts own genetics. IsletAgent decides what to retrieve and which analysis to run; the platform decides what can run. Training data: examples are generated from the same knowledge graph, using common question patterns, such as single-feature effects, donor-group differences, cross-omics agreement, prediction and single-entity profiles. Evidence is retrieved with the same functions the live system uses. Reference answers are written by code from that evidence, not by people or another language model. Each answer: cites every statistic it reports states the effect direction grades the support notes whether cohort and public evidence agree separates markers of cell composition from regulators of function says so when the evidence is not enough Checks: before training, every cohort statistic used as evidence was traced back to its source table. Evaluation: IsletAgent was tested on held-out questions about genes, metabolites and phenotypes it never saw in training. It was also tested on new questions written by islet researchers or taken from published papers. Both times it was compared with the same base model and with a larger untuned model. 7.4 Evidence grades IsletAgent grades the evidence for each relationship, not for a gene on its own. For example, ABCC8  insulin secretion and ABCC8  type 2 diabetes are graded separately. Evidence falls into three independent streams. Each has its own rules and a maximum, and the streams are added up. Cohort: association, prediction and correlation in the HumanIslets cohort, scored by the number of independent analytes. Transcript and protein count separately; RNA-seq and NanoString count as one transcript unit, and derived measurements add nothing beyond their source layers. Correlation counts only when there is no phenotype endpoint. Effect direction is reported (concordant, discordant or single-analyte) but does not change the score. Genetics: only the highest step of a ladder counts. The steps are QTL only, GWAS, QTL plus GWAS, colocalization, and colocalization with significant Mendelian randomization. QTL types are weighted by how directly they act on the gene: eQTL and pQTL most, then sQTL and exon-level eQTL, then caQTL. Extra credit is given for replication between local and external populations, for colocalization and Mendelian randomization that agree, and for GWAS signals in both local and public data. Knowledge: curated public relations, with more credit for relations specific to the target than for general ones. Knowledge is weighted below cohort data, because it reflects how widely a gene is annotated rather than replication. Provisional credit: when both ends of a link carry genetic evidence, the link gets provisional credit until the causal test is run. A significant result moves it to the top genetic step; a null result removes the credit. So a score can go down, and a measured null counts as evidence. Not applicable: a stream is scored only when it applies to both ends of a link. Otherwise it is marked not applicable, not zero. Metabolites, contaminants and lipids have no genetic links; feature-to-feature links get no genetics; and electrophysiology phenotypes, which have no GWAS, are graded on cohort evidence alone. The total maps to four grades: Limited, Moderate, Strong and Very Strong. Very Strong needs evidence from more than one stream or full genetic evidence. Limited reflects the amount of evidence, not its statistical strength, so a low grade means little evidence so far, not that a link is wrong. Grades are updated when a triggered analysis returns. The grading rules are checked by automated tests. In IsletAgent, the Evidence profile panel shows how much each stream contributes, against its maximum. The design follows the ClinGen genedisease validity framework (Strande NT, Riggs ER, Buchanan AH, et al. Evaluating the clinical validity of gene-disease associations: an evidence-based framework developed by the Clinical Genome Resource. Am J Hum Genet. 2017;100:895906. doi:10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.04.015). It differs in that grading is automatic, works at cohort scale, and can trigger new analyses and revise grades. The grades were checked against independent ClinGen classifications of monogenic diabetes genes.
